newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr edges higher, wage data a support.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr edges higher, wage data a support.

text.p: The Australian dollar edged higher at midday, helped by a bounce in US$/yen and firm wages data.
The Department of Industrial Relations released data on wage trends in enterprise bargains showing average annualised growth rose to 4.8 percent in the March quarter from 4.4 percent in Q4.
Analysts, especially those in the easing camp, cautioned the data covered only a tiny percentage of the workforce and weekly earnings data would be far more important for the rate outlook.
Those looking for steady policy noted the RBA did look at the DIR data and it had to be worrying that private sector deals had accelerated while unemployment was still around 8.5 percent.
By 11.45 am (0145 GMT) the dollar had crept to US$0.7748/53 from an early US$0.7734/39 and a US$0.7713 low offshore. It finished Tuesday at US$0.7741/46 here.

Traders said the bounce had proved the resilience of support beneath US$0.7720 and saw scope for a short covering rise toward US$0.7770 resistance near term and perhaps 78 cents if bears lost their nerve.

The drift upwards was encouraged by a much needed bounce in US$/yen which had regained ground to 113.80/85 yen after diving to 112.60 in the wake of the Federal Reserve's decision not to raise U.S. interest rates at its meeting overnight.

The local currency followed to stand at 88.27/37 yen from an early 87.07/17 but was still far short of the 90.00 level held at the end of last week, and a world away from the 100.00 high hit on May 1.

Traders said they were hearing the Japanese Ministry of Finance was trying to shore up US$/yen by telling Japanese institutions it was safe to invest in U.S. and offshore assets with the dollar above 112.00 yen. That echoed comments from MOF forex guru Eisuke Sakakibara the yen rise had been too rapid.
But it was too early to say US$/yen had stabilised and a break above 115.00 was needed to restore some confidence.
On the domestic front the market was still grappling with persistent speculation the Reserve Bank could yet ease interest rates.

The easing argument mainly hinged on the belief the recent wages growth which so alarmed the RBA had been biased up by special circumstances in the public sector and private deals were much more subdued.

Some expected proof of this to be provided by final average weekly earnings data on Thursday and were inclined to dismiss today's DIR survey as unrepresentative of the general trend, noting it covered less than three percent of all employees.
The data also did not take into account any productivity element of the pay deals.
Nevertheless, the fact that private deals rose faster than all sectors, where annual growth moved to 4.7 percent from 4.4 percent, put a questionmark over the easing camp's relaxed attitude to wages.

The growth rate for all current wage agreements also picked up to 4.8 percent from 4.6 percent in Q4 and these covered some 15 percent of all employees. This reading was the highest since enterprise bargaining began in 1991 and the measure has been trending up since the September quarter of 1994.
Australian Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith shared the reservations saying the data showed wage increases were too high for a low inflation environment.
The rate cut talk might yet grow if the final figures on Q1 average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) confirm suspicions private sector growth had not accelerated sharply.

The initial data showed a surprisingly strong rise in overall wages to an annual 4.6 percent from 3.9 percent in Q3, but analysts see a good chance annual growth in private deals will be under 3.5 percent.
